deep.reconstruction:
Context: Riemann's 1847 student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (published posthumously in the Werke, 1876). He seeks a generalised derivative of arbitrary order nu, written {}^x∂^ν_z. It is defined through a generalised Taylor expansion, series (2): z(x+h) = Σ_ν k_ν · {}^x∂^ν_z · h^ν, where ν runs over a progression ν0 + Z. This is to contain the ordinary Taylor series (1), z(x+h) = Σ_{n≥0} z^{(n)}(x) h^n / n!.

The page opens by finishing the remark after formula (3) of the previous page:
x^μ/Π(μ) = Σ_{α∈α0+Z} [b^{μ-α}/Π(μ-α)] · [(x-b)^α/Π(α)], with Π(s) = Γ(s+1).
When μ is a negative integer the left side is 0. So, he notes, there are series of this two-sided form that equal 0, or a constant, for every x.

My check of the zero case (mine, not on the page). Take μ = -1 and write t = (x-b)/b. The reflection formula gives Γ(-α)Γ(1+α) = -π/sin(πα). The right side then becomes -(sin(πα0)/π) · b^{-1} · t^{α0} · Σ_{k∈Z} (-t)^k. The two-sided geometric series diverges for every t. Formally, however, it sums to zero: 1/(1+t) + (-1/t)/(1+1/t) = 0. This explains his 'protest against the verdict passed on divergent series'.

Main argument of the page:
(i) The aim is that ordinary differentiation be a special case of the derivative of general order. This is achieved provided k_n = 1/n! for positive integers n and k_n = 0 for negative integers n. Then (2), with ν running over Z, reduces to (1).
(ii) Infinitely many functions k_ν satisfy this interpolation condition.
(iii) Two-sided series in powers of h need not have unique coefficient systems, because of the null series just exhibited. So one must allow infinitely many systems of coefficients for the same function.
(iv) There is therefore freedom both in k_ν and in the coefficient system. The choice should be made, where possible, so that the general-order derivatives obey laws otherwise valid only for integer orders.

The next page carries this out. Comparing d/dh with d/dx gives k_{ν+1}(ν+1) = k_ν, hence ∂^{ν+n} = d^n ∂^ν / dx^n, and c(ν) = Π(ν) k_ν is periodic with period 1. Then the index law ∂^ν ∂^μ = ∂^{ν+μ} is sought. The natural choice k_ν = 1/Γ(ν+1) satisfies everything in (i).
errors: No mathematical errors on this page; it is programmatic. The reduction of (2) to (1) holds only when ν runs over the integers; for a fractional offset ν0 the vanishing condition does not apply.
The non-uniqueness claim rests on formal (divergent) two-sided series. It is heuristically justified by the null series from (3), but not rigorously.

results.what: Two-sided generalised power series (from formula (3) with μ a negative integer) that formally sum to 0 or a constant, hence non-uniqueness of coefficients
results.modern_name: Formal two-sided (bilateral) series / null series; reflection formula of Gamma
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (formal sums of divergent series); Riemann's 1847 essay contains this remark

results.what: Interpolation condition k_n = 1/n! (n ≥ 0), k_n = 0 (n < 0) so that the generalised Taylor series contains the ordinary one; freedom of choice used to preserve integer-order laws
results.modern_name: Generalised Taylor series for fractional derivatives; 1/Γ(ν+1) as interpolant of 1/n!; Riemann–Liouville fractional calculus

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's 1847 fractional-calculus essay, published in his Collected Works (1876) and the source of the name Riemann–Liouville. The content is methodological and well known as his.

checkable.asserts: Reflection formula Γ(-α)Γ(1+α) = -π/sin(πα), used to rewrite (3) for μ = -1 (should give 0)
Formal two-sided geometric series Σ_{k∈Z} (-t)^k sums to 0 (the null series behind 'Reihen, die der Null gleich sind')
k_ν = 1/Γ(ν+1) equals 1/ν! at non-negative integers (list of zeros)
k_ν = 1/Γ(ν+1) vanishes at negative integers (list of zeros)
k_{ν+1}(ν+1) = k_ν for k_ν = 1/Γ(ν+1) (next page's condition; should give 0)

transcription_corrections: The words 'eine' (Entwicklung) and 'ein' (System) are underlined for emphasis in the manuscript.
k_ν appears written with a capital-looking K (K_ν) in the image; same quantity as k_ν on the next page.
'diese Bedingung kann ... genügt werden' — grammatically 'dieser Bedingung'; the manuscript reading is unclear, meaning unaffected.
The insertion 'wo möglich' is written above the line before 'Wahl'; correctly placed in the transcription.
